title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The being finished speaking and fixed his eyes on me, waiting for a reply. But I was overwhelmed, confused, and unable to fully grasp the scope of his demand. He continued,
"You must create a female for me, with whom I can share the companionship necessary for my existence. Only you can do this, and I demand it as a right you cannot refuse."
The latter part of his story had rekindled the anger that had faded while he described his peaceful life among the cottagers. When he finished, I could no longer suppress the rage burning inside me.

"I refuse," I replied. "No torture will ever wring consent from me. You may make me the most miserable of men, but you'll never make me betray my own principles. Shall I create another like you, whose combined wickedness might devastate the world? Get out! I've given you my answer. You may torture me, but I will never agree."

"You're wrong," the fiend replied, "and instead of threatening, I'm willing to reason with you. I'm cruel because I'm miserable. Am I not shunned and hated by all humanity? You, my creator, would tear me apart and celebrate. Remember that — and then tell me why I should pity mankind more than mankind pities me. You wouldn't call it murder if you could push me into one of these crevasses and destroy the body you made with your own hands. Should I respect people who condemn me? Let them live with me in mutual kindness, and instead of harm, I would shower them with every blessing, weeping tears of gratitude. But that can never be. Human senses are an insurmountable barrier between us. Yet I won't submit like a cringing slave. I'll take my revenge. If I can't inspire love, I'll cause fear — and above all toward you, my greatest enemy because you are my creator, I swear undying hatred. Be careful. I'll work toward your destruction until I've devastated your heart so completely that you'll curse the hour of your birth."
A fiendish rage animated him as he said this. His face contorted into expressions too horrible for human eyes. But he quickly calmed himself and continued —

"I meant to reason calmly. This passion harms me, because you don't realize that _you_ are its cause. If any being showed me kindness, I would return it a hundred and a hundredfold. For that one person's sake, I would make peace with the entire human race! But I'm dreaming of happiness I can never have. What I'm asking is reasonable and modest. I want a creature of the other sex, but as ugly as myself. The satisfaction is small, but it's all I can have, and it will be enough. It's true we'll be monsters, cut off from the world. But for that very reason we'll be more devoted to each other. Our lives won't be happy, but they'll be harmless and free from the misery I feel now. Oh, my creator, make me happy! Let me feel gratitude toward you for one kindness! Let me see that I can awaken sympathy in some living thing. Don't deny me my request!"

I was moved. I shuddered at the possible consequences of agreeing. But I felt there was justice in his argument. His story and the feelings he'd expressed proved him a creature of fine sensibilities. Didn't I, as his maker, owe him whatever happiness I could provide? He saw my change of feeling and continued,

"If you agree, neither you nor any other human being will ever see us again. I'll go to the vast wilderness of South America. My food isn't what humans eat. I don't slaughter lambs and goats to satisfy my hunger. Acorns and berries are enough for me. My companion will be of the same nature and content with the same food. We'll make our bed of dried leaves. The sun will shine on us as it does on everyone and ripen our food. The picture I'm painting is peaceful and human, and you must feel that you could deny it only out of a wanton abuse of power and cruelty. Pitiless as you've been toward me, I now see compassion in your eyes. Let me seize this moment and persuade you to promise what I so desperately desire."

"You propose," I replied, "to flee from civilization and live in the wilderness, where wild animals will be your only companions. How can you, who long for human love and connection, persist in this exile? You'll return and seek their kindness again — and meet their hatred. Your evil passions will be renewed. And you'll have a companion to help you destroy. This cannot be. Stop arguing. I cannot consent."

"How changeable your feelings are! Just a moment ago you were moved by my words. Why do you harden your heart against me again? I swear to you, by the earth I walk on and by you who made me, that with the companion you give me, I'll leave human society forever. I'll live, wherever chance takes me, in the most remote, savage places. My evil passions will have fled, because I'll have someone who understands me! My life will pass quietly, and in my final moments I won't curse my maker."

His words had a strange effect on me. I pitied him and sometimes felt a wish to console him. But when I looked at him — when I saw the filthy mass that moved and talked — my stomach turned and my feelings shifted to horror and revulsion. I tried to suppress these reactions. I thought that since I couldn't sympathize with him, I had no right to withhold the small measure of happiness still in my power to grant.
"You swear," I said, "to be harmless. But haven't you already shown enough cruelty to make me distrust you? Might this not be a trick to make your revenge even more devastating?"

"How is this? I won't be toyed with. I demand an answer. If I have no bonds and no love, hatred and evil must be my lot. Another's love will destroy the cause of my crimes. I'll become a being whose existence nobody even knows about. My vices are the children of a forced isolation I despise. My virtues will naturally emerge when I live with an equal. I'll feel the emotions of a conscious being and become linked to the chain of existence from which I'm now excluded."

I paused for a long time to reflect on everything he'd told me and the arguments he'd used. I thought of the promise of goodness he'd shown at the beginning of his life and how it had been destroyed by the hatred and contempt his protectors had shown him. His power and threats weren't lost on me either. A creature who could survive in ice caves and hide among inaccessible cliffs was a being I couldn't hope to fight. After a long pause, I concluded that justice — both to him and to my fellow humans — required me to agree to his request. Turning to him, I said,
"I consent to your demand, on your solemn oath to leave Europe forever — and every other place near human habitation — as soon as I deliver a female companion to you."

"I swear," he cried, "by the sun, and by the blue sky of heaven, and by the fire of love that burns in my heart — if you grant my prayer, you will never see me again while they exist. Go home and begin your work. I'll watch its progress with inexpressible anxiety. Don't worry — when you're ready, I shall appear."
With that, he suddenly left me, afraid, perhaps, that I might change my mind. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle and quickly vanish among the waves of the sea of ice.

His tale had taken the entire day. The sun was on the horizon when he departed. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness surrounded me. But my heart was heavy, and my steps slow. The struggle of winding among the narrow mountain paths, placing my feet carefully as I went, was made harder by the emotions the day's events had stirred. Night was far advanced when I reached the halfway resting place and sat down beside a fountain. Stars shone through gaps in the clouds. Dark pines rose before me. Here and there a fallen tree lay on the ground. It was a scene of solemn wonder that stirred strange thoughts. I wept bitterly. Clasping my hands in anguish, I cried, "Oh, stars and clouds and winds! Are you all about to mock me? If you truly pity me, crush my consciousness and memory. Let me become nothing. But if not — go away and leave me in darkness."

These were wild, miserable thoughts. I can't describe how the eternal twinkling of the stars weighed on me, or how I listened to every gust of wind as if it were a dull, ugly sirocco — the hot desert wind — on its way to consume me.

Morning broke before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest but returned immediately to Geneva. Even in my own heart I couldn't put my feelings into words. They pressed on me with the weight of a mountain and their sheer intensity destroyed my ability to feel their pain. So I returned home. Entering the house, I presented myself to my family. My wild, haggard appearance alarmed them intensely. But I answered no questions and barely spoke. I felt as if I were under a curse — as if I had no right to their sympathy, as if I could never again enjoy their companionship. Yet I loved them with utter devotion. To save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most hated task. The prospect of such work made everything else in my life pass before me like a dream. That thought alone felt real.
